raw_evidence.label: The two giants: Anthropic and OpenAI
raw_evidence.content: Two foundation-model companies tower over everyone else on cumulative capital raised. OpenAI (founded 2015, San Francisco) and Anthropic (founded 2021, San Francisco) together account for the majority of all money raised by the cohort. The dataset records OpenAI at roughly $182.6 B and Anthropic at $60 B in cumulative funding — figures that are point-in-time and have escalated rapidly: Anthropic's valuation alone climbed from about $61.5 B in March 2025 to $183 B that September, and OpenAI closed a round near an $852 B valuation in early 2026. The two are locked in a foundation-model rivalry that the rest of the list largely orbits.

raw_evidence.label: Funding leaderboard and the power-law skew
raw_evidence.content: Cumulative funding is extraordinarily top-heavy. The 50 companies have raised about $305.7 B combined, but OpenAI ($182.6 B) and Anthropic ($60 B) alone account for $242.6 B — 79.4% of all capital on the list. Add Databricks ($20 B), Cursor ($3.3 B) and Mistral AI ($3.1 B) and the top five hold 88.0% of the total. The mean raise is $6,113 M but the median is just $735 M, an 8.3× gap that is the signature of a power-law distribution: a few giants and a long tail. This is a near-perfect picture of an AI gold rush where capital concentrates at the foundation-model frontier.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_02 ===")
ranked = sorted(records, key=lambda r: (r["funding_m"] if r["funding_m"] is not None else -1), reverse=True)
total = sum(funds)
print(f"total cohort funding = {total:,.1f} M  (= ${total/1000:,.2f} B)")
import statistics as st
print(f"mean = {st.mean(funds):,.1f} M ; median = {st.median(funds):,.1f} M")
top2 = ranked[:2]
top2_sum = sum(r["funding_m"] for r in top2)
print(f"top 2 = {[r['name'] for r in top2]} = {top2_sum:,.1f} M = {100*top2_sum/total:.1f}% of total")
top5_sum = sum(r["funding_m"] for r in ranked[:5])
print(f"top 5 share = {100*top5_sum/total:.1f}%")
print("Full leaderboard (name, $M):")
for r in ranked:
    print(f"  {r['name']:<24} {r['funding_m']:>9,.0f}")

top 5 share = 88.0%

The list is really two lists stacked: a couple of generational outliers, and four dozen well-funded but ordinary-by-comparison startups.

raw_evidence.label: Funding leaderboard and the power-law skew
raw_evidence.content: Cumulative funding is extraordinarily top-heavy. The 50 companies have raised about $305.7 B combined, but OpenAI ($182.6 B) and Anthropic ($60 B) alone account for $242.6 B — 79.4% of all capital on the list. Add Databricks ($20 B), Cursor ($3.3 B) and Mistral AI ($3.1 B) and the top five hold 88.0% of the total. The mean raise is $6,113 M but the median is just $735 M, an 8.3× gap that is the signature of a power-law distribution: a few giants and a long tail. This is a near-perfect picture of an AI gold rush where capital concentrates at the foundation-model frontier.
raw_evidence.code:

print(f"top 5 share = {100*top5_sum/total:.1f}%")
print("Full leaderboard (name, $M):")
for r in ranked:

The list is really two lists stacked: a couple of generational outliers, and four dozen well-funded but ordinary-by-comparison startups.

raw_evidence.label: Age vs funding — youth is no barrier
raw_evidence.content: Older companies are not the best-funded ones; if anything the correlation between founding year and funding is slightly negative (Pearson r = -0.285). Broken into eras, the 2013-2018 cohort has a huge mean ($16,311 M) but that is entirely OpenAI and Databricks distorting it — its median is $850 M. The 2022-2025 cohort (28 companies) has a median of $668 M, not far below the older groups, despite being only a few years old. In this market, capital flows to perceived frontier potential, not to seniority: Thinking Machines Lab raised $2 B founded in 2025, while plenty of 2016-2018 companies sit under $1 B.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_10 ===")
pairs = [(r["year"], r["funding_m"], r["name"]) for r in records if r["year"] and r["funding_m"] is not None]
# correlation
import math
xs = [p[0] for p in pairs]; ys = [p[1] for p in pairs]
mx, my = st.mean(xs), st.mean(ys)
cov = sum((x-mx)*(y-my) for x,y in zip(xs,ys))/len(xs)
sx = st.pstdev(xs); sy = st.pstdev(ys)
corr = cov/(sx*sy) if sx and sy else 0
print(f"Pearson corr(year, funding) = {corr:.3f} (n={len(pairs)})")
# median funding by founding-era bucket
def era(y):
    if y <= 2018: return "2013-2018"
    if y <= 2021: return "2019-2021"
    return "2022-2025"
eras = defaultdict(list)
for y,f,nm in pairs:
    eras[era(y)].append(f)
for e in ["2013-2018","2019-2021","2022-2025"]:
    v = eras[e]
    print(f"  {e}: n={len(v)} median=${st.median(v):,.0f}M mean=${st.mean(v):,.0f}M")
# line 226

  2013-2018: n=13 median=$850M mean=$16,311M

  2022-2025: n=28 median=$668M mean=$1,019M

raw_evidence.label: What they actually do — the category map
raw_evidence.content: Sorting all 50 companies by what they build reveals a list dominated by applied AI, not just labs. The biggest category is generative media (8 companies: image, video, voice, music — ElevenLabs, Runway, Suno, Synthesia, Midjourney, Black Forest Labs, HeyGen, Krea), followed by foundation models (7) and AI infrastructure & chips (7, including Databricks, SambaNova, Together AI, Crusoe). Then come AI agents for customer-service/GTM/knowledge work (6), coding & app builders (5), robotics & autonomy (4), and clusters of three in healthcare, legal & finance, and data labeling. The long tail — search (Perplexity), productivity (Notion), security (Cyera), a voice tutor (Speak) — fills out the rest. Applied verticals outnumber the model labs roughly six to one.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_07 ===")
CAT = {
    "Foundation models": ["Anthropic","OpenAI","Cohere","Mistral AI","Reflection","Safe Superintelligence","Thinking Machines Lab"],
    "Coding & app builders": ["Cognition","Cursor","Replit","Lovable","Gamma"],
    "Generative media": ["Black Forest Labs","ElevenLabs","HeyGen","Krea","Midjourney","Runway","Suno","Synthesia"],
    "Agents (CS / GTM / knowledge)": ["Clay","Decagon","Genspark.ai","Glean","Sierra","EliseAI"],
    "Healthcare": ["Abridge","Chai Discovery","OpenEvidence"],
    "Legal & finance": ["Harvey","Legora","Rogo"],
    "Robotics & autonomy": ["Applied Intuition","Physical Intelligence","Skild AI","World Labs"],
    "AI infrastructure & chips": ["Baseten","Crusoe","Fal","Fireworks AI","SambaNova","Together AI","Databricks"],
    "Search": ["Perplexity"],
    "Data labeling / research data": ["Mercor","Surge AI","Listen Labs"],
    "Productivity": ["Notion"],
    "Security": ["Cyera"],
    "Education / voice tutor": ["Speak"],
}
# verify every company assigned exactly once
assigned = {}
for cat, names in CAT.items():
    for nm in names:
        assigned[nm] = cat
missing = [r["name"] for r in records if r["name"] not in assigned]
print("unassigned:", missing)
catcount = Counter(assigned[r["name"]] for r in records if r["name"] in assigned)
for c, n in catcount.most_common():
    print(f"  {c:<32} {n}")
print(f"total categorized: {sum(catcount.values())}/{N}")
# funding by category
catfund = defaultdict(float)
for r in records:
    if r["name"] in assigned and r["funding_m"] is not None:
        catfund[assigned[r["name"]]] += r["funding_m"]
print("funding by category ($M):")
for c, f in sorted(catfund.items(), key=lambda x:-x[1]):
    print(f"  {c:<32} {f:>10,.0f}")

raw_evidence.label: Funding leaderboard and the power-law skew
raw_evidence.content: Cumulative funding is extraordinarily top-heavy. The 50 companies have raised about $305.7 B combined, but OpenAI ($182.6 B) and Anthropic ($60 B) alone account for $242.6 B — 79.4% of all capital on the list. Add Databricks ($20 B), Cursor ($3.3 B) and Mistral AI ($3.1 B) and the top five hold 88.0% of the total. The mean raise is $6,113 M but the median is just $735 M, an 8.3× gap that is the signature of a power-law distribution: a few giants and a long tail. This is a near-perfect picture of an AI gold rush where capital concentrates at the foundation-model frontier.

raw_evidence.label: The founding surge — born yesterday
raw_evidence.content: These are strikingly young companies. 34 of 50 (68%) were founded in 2020 or later, and 28 of 50 (56%) in 2022 or later — after the late-2022 ChatGPT moment that detonated the generative-AI boom. 2022 is the single biggest founding year with 11 companies, followed closely by 2023 with 10; together those two years alone produced 21 of the 50. The oldest company is Databricks (2013) and the newest is Thinking Machines Lab (2025), already valued enough to make the list within months of its founding. The AI 50 is less a hall of fame than a snapshot of a wave that crested in the last three years.

raw_evidence.label: What they actually do — the category map
raw_evidence.content: Sorting all 50 companies by what they build reveals a list dominated by applied AI, not just labs. The biggest category is generative media (8 companies: image, video, voice, music — ElevenLabs, Runway, Suno, Synthesia, Midjourney, Black Forest Labs, HeyGen, Krea), followed by foundation models (7) and AI infrastructure & chips (7, including Databricks, SambaNova, Together AI, Crusoe). Then come AI agents for customer-service/GTM/knowledge work (6), coding & app builders (5), robotics & autonomy (4), and clusters of three in healthcare, legal & finance, and data labeling. The long tail — search (Perplexity), productivity (Notion), security (Cyera), a voice tutor (Speak) — fills out the rest. Applied verticals outnumber the model labs roughly six to one.

raw_evidence.label: Funding leaderboard and the power-law skew
raw_evidence.content: Cumulative funding is extraordinarily top-heavy. The 50 companies have raised about $305.7 B combined, but OpenAI ($182.6 B) and Anthropic ($60 B) alone account for $242.6 B — 79.4% of all capital on the list. Add Databricks ($20 B), Cursor ($3.3 B) and Mistral AI ($3.1 B) and the top five hold 88.0% of the total. The mean raise is $6,113 M but the median is just $735 M, an 8.3× gap that is the signature of a power-law distribution: a few giants and a long tail. This is a near-perfect picture of an AI gold rush where capital concentrates at the foundation-model frontier.

raw_evidence.label: The founding surge — born yesterday
raw_evidence.content: These are strikingly young companies. 34 of 50 (68%) were founded in 2020 or later, and 28 of 50 (56%) in 2022 or later — after the late-2022 ChatGPT moment that detonated the generative-AI boom. 2022 is the single biggest founding year with 11 companies, followed closely by 2023 with 10; together those two years alone produced 21 of the 50. The oldest company is Databricks (2013) and the newest is Thinking Machines Lab (2025), already valued enough to make the list within months of its founding. The AI 50 is less a hall of fame than a snapshot of a wave that crested in the last three years.

raw_evidence.label: What the AI 50 is and who builds it
raw_evidence.content: The Forbes AI 50 is an annual editorial list of the most promising privately held companies building artificial intelligence, produced by Forbes in partnership with Sequoia Capital and Meritech Capital. The 2025 edition is the seventh annual list. Companies are selected through a proprietary algorithm plus editorial judgment that weighs business promise, AI sophistication and real-world impact; only private companies are eligible, so public AI giants (Nvidia, Microsoft, Google) are excluded by construction. This is therefore a curated snapshot of the private AI frontier at a single moment in 2025, not a complete census of the industry.

raw_evidence.label: Caveats — a curated, point-in-time, rounded snapshot
raw_evidence.content: Several caveats govern any reading of this dataset. It is a curated editorial list of private companies only, so it omits public AI leaders and any private company Forbes' algorithm did not surface. Funding figures are cumulative capital raised, rounded (e.g. '$830 M', '$60 B'), and point-in-time — they were already stale within months given the pace of AI rounds. Two entries record '$0 M' (Midjourney and Surge AI), reflecting famously bootstrapped or non-disclosed companies rather than literally zero capital. Founding years cluster tightly in the last decade, and 'What It Does' is a one-line editorial gloss, not a formal taxonomy. The data is best read as a careful sketch of the private AI frontier, not a precise ledger.

Add Databricks ($20 B), Cursor ($3.3 B) and Mistral AI ($3.1 B) and the top five hold 88.0% of the total. The mean raise is $6,113 M but the median is just $735 M, an 8.3× gap that is the signature of a power-law distribution: a few giants and a long tail. This is a near-perfect picture of an AI gold rush where capital concentrates at the foundation-model frontier.
